meta.title: Vahiny Mianatra Malagasy — Full Content Pack
meta.description: Unified dataset for the website & app: vocabulary, phrases, dialogues, grammar, pronunciation and cultural notes for a beginner English-speaking elderly learner. Official Malagasy with Tsimihety dialect variants.
sources: Comprehensive Malagasy vocabulary and phrase dataset
Grammar rules and sentence structures for English speakers
Pronunciation guides and regional greeting variants

vowels.sound: like 'dz' (as in BRIDGE), NOT like English 'j'

notes: There is no verb 'to be' — pronouns alone carry it: 'aho' means both 'I' and 'I am'.
No grammatical gender, no verb conjugation by person: mihinana (eat) → nihinana (ate) → hihinana (will eat); only the first letter changes.
The Malagasy alphabet has no c, q, u, w, x.
Malagasy sentence order is Verb + Object + Subject: 'Mihinana vary aho' literally = 'Eats rice I' = I eat rice.
Stress is usually on the next-to-last syllable.

rules.rule: Malagasy sentence structure is PREDICATE–SUBJECT
rules.explanation: A complete sentence has two basic elements: SUBJECT (a person, thing or place which the sentence revolves around) and PREDICATE (the part of the sentence that complements the subject). In Malagasy sentences the SUBJECT is not at the start of the sentence. In English we say 'Polly is happy', but in Malagasy it becomes 'Happy is Polly'.

rules.rule: The PREDICATE can be a NOUN, a NUMBER, an ADJECTIVE, an ADVERB, a VERB, etc.
rules.explanation: Unlike English, the predicate in Malagasy is not restricted to a verb.

rules.rule: Malagasy nouns have no gender
rules.explanation: Particularly for French speakers: Malagasy nouns do not have gender, so there is no need for the predicate to follow the subject in grammatical gender.

rules.rule: Question form when the predicate is an ADJECTIVE
rules.explanation: Use MANAHOANA ny…? / MANAKORY ny…?

rules.rule: Question form when asking about the SUBJECT/OBJECT
rules.explanation: Use INONA no…? / INO…?

rules.rule: Question form when the subject is a PERSON
rules.explanation: Use IZA no…? / ZOVY…?

rules.rule: The particle VE or MOA poses a yes/no question
rules.explanation: …Ve…? / …Moa…? — answered with 'Ia, …' (yes) or 'Ehe, tsy…' (no).

rules.rule: Question words are chosen according to the type of predicate
rules.explanation: MANAHOANA/MANAKORY = HOW; INONA/INO = WHAT; IZA/ZOVY = WHO; VE/MOA = question particles.

rules.rule: The sentence structure is PREDICATE–SUBJECT, where the predicate is an intransitive verb
rules.explanation: An intransitive verb is a verb that does not require a complement. In Malagasy, verbs always remain the same while the subject changes. Since there is no gender or number, there is no need for agreement between the verb and the subject, unlike European languages in general.

rules.rule: Tense marking: indicative verbs starting with 'M' change M to 'N' for the past and 'H' for the future
rules.explanation: The M/N/H initial letter of the verb provides a sense of time.

rules.rule: Negation: add TSY before the verb
rules.explanation: TSY is the negation particle placed directly before the verb.

examples.en: He works -> He does not work
I worked -> I did not work

examples.mg: Hiasa I Soa -> Tsy hiasa I Soa
examples.en: Soa will work -> Soa will not work

rules.rule: The subject can be a pronoun or a noun
rules.explanation: Same verb form with every subject pronoun (official Malagasy in parentheses).

rules.rule: Forming questions with Manino / Zovy / Ino / Ve
rules.explanation: Manino (Maninona, official) = What are we doing?; Zovy (iza no) = Who is?; Ino (inona no) = What is?; Ve = Is it / Do…?

rules.explanation: The direct object could be a noun, pronoun, person, object, or animal. Structure: Transitive verb – Object – Subject.

rules.rule: For intransitive verbs, the structure is Verb – Subject

rules.explanation: Efa = already; mbola tsy = not yet; mbola = still; efa tsy = no longer. These come at the beginning of the predicate phrase.

rules.rule: A demonstrative is an adjective or pronoun used to point out a person or object; the form changes based on number and distance
rules.explanation: Ity/Ireto (this/these): used for objects or people held in hand or pointed at. Iny/Ireny (that/those): used for distant objects or people, or those held by another person. Itsy/Iretsy/Irý/Irerý (that/those): often answered with io/ireo (that/those) in questions.

examples.en: What is that? → That is a shoe.
Who are those? → They are teachers.

rules.rule: Distance forms of demonstratives (singular / plural)
rules.explanation: Near: ity / ireto (off), tôho / ireto (tsm). Intermediate: io / ireo (both). Farther: itsy / iretsy (off), rôho / rôho (tsm). Farther still: irý / irerý (off), rôho / rôho (tsm). Very far: iny / ireny (both, off and tsm).

rules.rule: Demonstrative adjectives: Demonstrative + Noun + Demonstrative
Demonstrative pronouns: Noun + Demonstrative

rules.rule: A – The Duplicative: the root of the predicate is repeated to form a comparative
rules.explanation: In the Tsimihety dialect, comparison can be expressed by duplication of the predicate. General rule: the root of the word is repeated. However, words ending in -KA, -TRA, or -NA follow special grammatical rules (irregular).

rules.rule: First-letter changes in the duplicated form
rules.explanation: l → d; v → b; s → ts; r → dr (e.g. maVesatra → mavesaBesatra).

rules.rule: Duplication can change a word's meaning positively or negatively
rules.explanation: If the word has a negative meaning, it becomes more positive when duplicated, and vice versa: ratsy (bad) → ratsiratsy (less bad) → tsara (good); manintsy (cold) → manintsinintsy (colder) → mafana (hot). However, comparatives in the Tsimihety dialect don't always follow the same change in meaning that the duplication would suggest.

rules.rule: B – The Comparative (Tsimihety dialect) with tsitoko

rules.rule: Instead of prepositions (to, with, from) before a noun, Malagasy changes the form of the pronoun itself

rules.rule: Sentence patterns with indirect pronouns
rules.explanation: Intransitive: Intransitive verb — indirect pronoun — subject. Transitive: Transitive verb — object — indirect pronoun — subject.

examples.en: He explains a lesson to the students. (transitive pattern)

rules.rule: In the past tense, the verb changes to past form (M to N), and the indirect pronoun gains a T at the front
rules.explanation: He works with us → Miaraka miasa aminay izy. He worked with us → Niaraka niasa taminay izy.

rules.rule: Indirect personal pronoun forms
rules.explanation: Aho/Zaho (I): AMIKO (off present) / TAMIKO (off past) / AMINAHY (tsm present) / TAMINAHY (tsm past). Ianao/Anao (you sg.): AMINAO/TAMINAO (off), AMINA(O)/TAMINA(O) (tsm). Izy (he/she): AMINY/TAMINY (off), AMINAZY/TAMINAZY (tsm). Isika/Antsika (we incl.): AMINTSIKA/TAMINTSIKA (both). Izahay/Zahay (we excl.): AMINAY/TAMINAY (both). Ianareo/Areo (you pl.): AMINAREO/TAMINAREO (off), AMINARE(O)/TAMINARE(O) (tsm). Izy ireo/Zareo (they): AMIN'IZY IREO/TAMIN'IZY IREO (off), AMINJARE(O)/TAMINJARE(O) (tsm). I Lita: AMIN'I LITA/TAMIN'I LITA (both forms). Ny dokotera: AMIN'NY DOKOTERA/TAMIN'NY DOKOTERA (both forms).

rules.rule: 1. A special group of words does not follow the general grammatical rules
rules.explanation: These are words that (a) have 3 or more syllables and (b) end in -KA, -TRA, or -NA. For all ordinary Malagasy words, the stress falls on the penultimate syllable (second to last). But for this special group, the stress falls on the antepenultimate syllable (third to last). The position of the stress is very important for both pronunciation and comprehension.

rules.rule: 2. Possession is marked by a personal pronoun suffix added to the noun
rules.explanation: The possessive expresses the relationship between people, or indicates to whom something belongs. Malagasy nouns have no gender and no number, so possessives are invariable — they do not agree with the noun. Structure: Noun (the thing possessed) + suffix (the possessor).

examples.mg: Ny maso (eye/eyes) + zaho (tsm, I) → Ny masoKO (my eye / my eyes)

rules.rule: 3. Rules for adding possessive suffixes depend on how the noun ends
rules.explanation: If the noun does not end in -KA, -TRA, or -NA: add the suffixes directly: ko, nao, ny, ntsika, nay, nareo, n'izy ireo, n'i Soa, n'ny ankizy. If the noun ends in -NA: drop the -NA ending, then add the same suffixes. If the noun ends in -TRA or -KA: drop the final -a (or the full -ka/-tra ending), then add the suffixes. Tsimihety uses different suffixes as it is a dialect.

rules.rule: 4. Possessive suffix table (with sample nouns: maso = eye (no special ending), tànaNA = hand (ends -NA), mpianaTRA = student (ends -TRA), satroKA = hat (ends -KA))

Izy 'he/she': masoNY / masoANAZY; tànaNY / tànagnANAZY; mpianaNY / mpianatrANAZY; satroNY / satrokOANAZY. Isika/antsika 'we (incl.)': masoNTSIKA / masoANTSIKA; tànaNTSIKA / tànagnANTSIKA; mpianaTSIKA / mpianatrANTSIKA; satroTSIKA / satrokoANTSIKA. rules.rule: The adverbial phrase of place indicates where someone is or where an action takes place; it answers AIZA / TAIZA (past) = 'where?'
rules.explanation: The place name is always preceded by a word called a 'locative'. The locative specifies the location — whether the place is near or far, visible or not, and whether the speaker is at that place or not. In the past tense, a 'T' is added to the front of the locative. Structure: Locative + Place name.

examples.en: Here in Madagascar — the speaker is in Madagascar (eto = here)
There in Madagascar — the speaker is away from Madagascar (any = there/over there)

rules.rule: Locatives differ by distance and visibility
rules.explanation: Visible location — on the spot 'here': eto (off) / aketo (tsm); ato (off) / akato (tsm) [non-visible]. A little further away 'there': eo (off) / akeo (tsm) [visible]; etsy/erȳ (off) / arôho (tsm), ao (off) / akao (tsm), atsy/arȳ (off) / arôho (tsm). Further away or very far 'there': eny (visible), any (off) / akany (tsm).

rules.rule: Group 1 — Proper place names: Locative + Place name
rules.explanation: Proper place names such as Madagasikara, Frantsa, Angletera, Mandritsara take the locative directly.

examples.en: over there in France — over there in England (speaker in Madagascar)
here in Madagascar — here in Mandritsara

rules.rule: Group 2 — Common place nouns: Locative + AN- + place noun (Locative + AM- before p or b)
rules.explanation: Common place nouns such as trano (house), lālana (street), fiangonana (church), zaridaina (garden). Consonant changes: f → p, l → d, s → ts, z → j, r → dr, h → k, v → b.

examples.en: (it was) over there in the garden [past]

rules.rule: Group 3 — Specific places or foreign-origin names: Locative + AMIN'NY + place noun
rules.explanation: Words such as Banky (bank), Hôpitaly (hospital), Bazary (market), Fiangonana Loteriana (Lutheran church).

examples.en: (it was) over there at the Lutheran church [past]

rules.rule: Structure of the adverbial phrase of place (CCL): Locative — Place
rules.explanation: TSY = negation; Mô = ve (question particle, 'is it…? / are…?').

rules.rule: Pattern 1: (TSY) — CCL — Subject

examples.en: Are you here at the hospital?

rules.explanation: MISY = there is / there are.

rules.rule: The adverbial phrase of time indicates when an action takes place
rules.explanation: Position: in Malagasy the subject comes at the end of the sentence, and the adverbial phrase of time is the only word or group of words that can come after the subject. Structure: Predicate — Subject — Adverbial Phrase of Time.

rules.rule: Agreement: predicates do not agree with gender or number, but the verb and adjective agree with the tense
rules.explanation: When the time word is introduced by the preposition amin'ny, it stays the same in the future but becomes tamin'ny in the past.

examples.en: It will be hot tomorrow — FUTURE

rules.rule: Time words: days relative to today (no preposition)
rules.explanation: Afak'omaly = the day before yesterday; omaly = yesterday; androany / anio = today; rahampitso = tomorrow; afaka rahampitso = the day after tomorrow. (The source also lists Tsimihety forms nomoaligny = yesterday, niagny = today, amaraigny = tomorrow, afaka nomoaligny, afaka amaraigny.)

rules.rule: Times of day: introduced by amin'ny … (tamin'ny … in the past)
rules.explanation: maraina (off) / maraindraigny (tsm) = morning; atoandro (off) / matsagna (tsm) = midday / noon; tolakandro (off) / folakandro (tsm) = afternoon; hariva (off) / harivariva (tsm) = evening; alina (off) / aligny (tsm) = night.

rules.rule: Days of the week: introduced by amin'ny … (tamin'ny … in the past)
rules.explanation: alatsinainy (off) / tinainy (tsm) = Monday; talata (both) = Tuesday; alarobia (off) / robiā (tsm) = Wednesday; alakamisy (off) / kamisy (tsm) = Thursday; zomā (off) / zomā / jomoā (tsm) = Friday; asabotsy (off) / sabôtsy (tsm) = Saturday; alahady (off) / lahady / dimansy (tsm) = Sunday.

rules.rule: Questions answering 'When?'
rules.explanation: Past: Oviana no …? (off) / Tafiriagna …? (tsm). Future: Rahoviana no …? (off) / Hafiriagna …? (tsm).

rules.rule: Months take amin'ny volana … (tamin'ny volana … in the past); French month names are also commonly used (e.g. Volana Août = the month of August)
rules.explanation: zanvie (off) / zanvie (tsm) = January; fevrie (off) / fevrie (tsm) = February; marsa (off) = March; avrily (off) = April; mey = May; jona (off) / jona (tsm) = June; jolay = July; aogositra = August; septambra = September; oktobra (off) / oktobra (tsm) = October; novambra = November; desambra = December. rules.rule: This week / this month / this year — past, present, future forms
rules.explanation: Week (herinandro off / vôlagna-related tsm): past = tamin'ny herinandro lasa (off) / tamin'ny herinandro teo igny (tsm); present = amin'ity herinandro ity (off) / amin'ny herinandro tôho (tsm); future = amin'ny herinandro ho avy (off) / amin'ny herinandro io / rôho (tsm). Month (volana off / vôlagna tsm): past = tamin'ny volana lasa / tamin'ny vôlagna teo igny; present = amin'ity volana ity / amin'ny vôlagna tôho; future = amin'ny volana ho avy / amin'ny vôlagna io / rôho. Year (taona off / taogno tsm): past = tamin'ny taona lasa / tamin'ny taogno teo igny; present = amin'ity taona ity / amin'ny taogno tôho; future = amin'ny taona ho avy / amin'ny taogno io / rôho. NB. You can use VOALOHANY (beginning) and FARANY (end) with week, month and year: Voalohan'ny herinandro = beginning of the week; Faran'ny volana = end of the month.

rules.rule: Time expressions answering 'How often?'
rules.explanation: Question: Isaky ny inona no …? (off) / Isaka ino …? (tsm) — 'How often…?'. Isaky ny maraina (off) / isaka maraindraigny (tsm) = every morning; isaky ny Alarobia (off) / isaka Robiā (tsm) = every Wednesday; isaky ny volana Janoary (off) / isaka vôlagna Zanvie (tsm) = every January; isan'andro (both) = every day; isan-kerinandro (off) / isaka herinandro (tsm) = every week; isam-bolana (off) / isam-bôlagna (tsm) = every month; isan-taona (off) / isan-taogno (tsm) = every year.

examples.en: How often does he have time off? — Every Wednesday afternoon.

examples.en: How often does he eat rice? — Every day. [tsm]

rules.explanation: Present/Future: Amin'ny firy no …? (off) / Amin'ny firy …? (tsm). Past: Tamin'ny firy no …? (off) / Tamin'ny firy …? (tsm).

rules.rule: Meal vocabulary (tsm)
rules.explanation: Homagna maraindraigny = to have breakfast (lit. to eat in the morning); homagna matsagna = to have lunch (lit. to eat at midday); homagna amin'ny aligny = to have dinner (lit. to eat at night).

rules.rule: Annexe — Adjective agreement with tense
rules.explanation: Adjectives starting with M-: past N- (nafana), present M- (mafana), future H- (hafana). Two-syllable words with M-: past N- (tsm) / — (off) (nora, tsm), present M- (mora), future Ho- (ho mora). Adjectives with other initial consonants: past — (faly), present the root (faly), future Ho- (ho faly).

examples.mg: Nora ny manga (tsm) / Mora ny manga (off)

examples.en: The child was happy (past '—') / is happy (present)
The child will be happy (future Ho-)

rules.rule: Annexe — Verb agreement with tense
rules.explanation: M- verbs: past N- (niasa), present M- (miasa), future H- (hiasa). Other consonant-initial verbs: past No- (nosasana), present root (sasana), future Ho- (hosasana). Root-type verbs: past — (tonga ny vahiny 'the visitor had arrived'), present root (tonga 'has arrived'), future Ho- (ho tonga 'will arrive'). Vowel-initial verbs: past N- (natao), present root (atao), future H- (hatao).

examples.en: The visitor had arrived (past) / has arrived (present)

grammar.title: The Absolute Minimum Grammar (from the 12-week curriculum)

rules.rule: There is no verb 'to be'
rules.explanation: Pronouns carry it: 'Aho' = I / I am; 'Mpampianatra aho' = I am a teacher.

rules.rule: Word order is Verb + Object + Subject
rules.explanation: Mihinana (eats) vary (rice) aho (I) — the subject goes at the END of the sentence.

rules.rule: Negation with 'tsy'
rules.explanation: Put 'tsy' at the start of the sentence to negate it.

rules.rule: Tense by first letter only
rules.explanation: Present M-, past N-, future H-: mihinana → nihinana → hihinana. No person conjugation.

rules.rule: No grammatical gender, no plurals
rules.explanation: One word for he/she (izy); nouns don't change for plural — context does the work.

rules.rule: Possession with suffixes
rules.explanation: Add -ko (my), -nao (your), -ny (his/her) to the noun: tranoko = my house.

examples.en: my house, your house, his/her house

rules.rule: 'Ve' makes a yes/no question
rules.explanation: Place 've' before the subject at the end: 'Amerikana ve ianao?'

rules.rule: Adjectives precede the noun
rules.explanation: ADJECTIVE + NOUN, no 'is/are' needed.

rules.rule: Inclusive vs exclusive 'we'
rules.explanation: isika = we including you; izahay = we excluding you. English has one 'we'; Malagasy has two. Use isika when talking with your teacher.

rules.rule: Demonstratives: ity (this near me), io (that near you), iris (that far)
rules.explanation: 'ity' = this (near me); 'io' = that (near you); 'iry' = that over there.

rules.rule: Numbers are read right-to-left
rules.explanation: 21 = iraika ambin'ny roapolo (one-and-twenty). Use 'ambin'ny' or 'amby' up to 199, 'sy' above.

rules.rule: 'Tsy misy' = there isn't / nothing
rules.explanation: 'tsy misy' means nothing/there isn't; 'tsy' alone just negates a verb.

lessons.title: Greetings (Introduction-Lesson 1a)
grammar_notes: Tsy = no/not; Tsisy = nothing.
Tsy precedes verbs/adjectives, whereas tsisy is usually preceded by a (i.e. combined with a) noun.
More grammar rules are introduced in subsequent lessons.
cultural_notes: Bako, the tutor, has been a language tutor in Mandritsara since 2008, teaching missionaries and visitors to the Hopitaly Vaovao Mahafaly project.
The dialect spoken in Mandritsara is called Tsimihety, but official Malagasy is widely spoken there as well.
In Mandritsara the most common way of greeting each other is by saying 'Salama Tompoko', literally 'hello, sir'.
When one arrives at a friend's house, the guest initiates the greeting at the door by saying out loud 'Haody!', much like a knock on the door.
A 'Kabary' is where both the guest and host take turns to give a short speech.

Malagasy Kabary originated as a highly poeticised speech performed in front of an audience. Today it is an integral part of social life, used in social events like festivities, ceremonies and funerals. Informally, people use it to convey thanks or welcome at dinner parties or gatherings.
If a guest is invited to a meal, the host never asks 'in vaovao' (what's new), as the intention for the visit is obvious.
There are 18 tribes spread across 22 regions in Madagascar.
Other ways of saying hello in Madagascar vary by region: 'Manao ahoana' (Central, e.g. Tana), 'Salama' (North/Central), 'Akory' (East/South), 'Miarahaba' (Central).

lessons.title: Saying goodbye (Introduction-Lesson 1b)
grammar_notes: Indray = koa, and the two can be used interchangeably (both mean 'again').
To specify a time when you will meet again, add the word 'again' ('koa' or 'indray') at the END of the sentence, e.g. 'Veloma/Mazotoa + [time] + koa'.
This formula extends to days in the future or specific days of the week: 'Veloma/Mazotoa + Alarobia koa' = see you on Wednesday.

For brevity you can drop 'veloma/mazotoa' and simply say the time when you will meet again followed by 'koa', e.g. 'Amin'ny alina koa' (see you tonight), 'Amarainy koa' (see you tomorrow), 'Talata koa' (see you on Tuesday).
Don't forget to add the word 'koa' at the end of the sentence!
cultural_notes: There are a number of ways to say goodbye in Malagasy; the most common are 'Veloma tompoko', 'Veloma e', 'Mazotoa', and 'Amin'ny manaraka indray'.
In Tsimihety, sometimes the 'n' consonant has a nasal sound which can be written as n̈ or ñ. In these lesson notes it is spelled 'gn' for convenience (e.g. volagna, taogno, amaraigny).

parts_of_the_day.cultural_note: Parts of day are relative to the position of the sun: 'Morning' = sunrise to late morning; 'Noon' = late morning to midday; 'Early afternoon' = midday to early afternoon; 'Afternoon' = the rest of the afternoon before sunset; 'Night' = sunset till sunrise.

lessons.title: Useful expressions (Introduction-Lesson 2)
grammar_notes: 'Azafady' is a very versatile word: its meaning depends on context (walking past someone, apologising for a mistake, or 'excuse me' at the start of a sentence).
'Mazotoa' is likewise very versatile, like azafady - it covers 'enjoy', 'have a good day', 'keep it up'.
'Tonga soa' (welcome) is formed by combining the words for 'arrived' (tonga) and 'well' (soa).
'Soava dia' (bon voyage) builds on 'soa' + 'dia' (journey).
cultural_notes: Although 'misaotra' is sufficient, saying 'MISAOTRA BETSAKA' is more polite.
You will invariably hear the word 'azafady' used a lot; it is an extremely useful word.

Body language (giving/receiving a gift): one usually stretches out both hands to express politeness. In Mandritsara, when one gives something or says 'misaotra', one usually bends the knee slightly as a sign of reverence.
Body language (walking past people): slightly bow your body and stretch your right hand out.
'MIALA TSINY' is another way of apologising over something trivial. For a serious offence you would literally be asking for forgiveness: 'MIFONA'. This is the term used in the Bible.
When invited with 'mandroso' to join a meal, the person is definitely not obliged to sit down and eat; they can simply respond 'Misaotra, mazotoa'.

proverbs.en_literal: We can share a cricket between us
proverbs.meaning: An expression of joy in sharing food - not about how delicious it is; it's okay if you're not into exotic delicacies.

proverbs.en_literal: The meal is ready for everyone
proverbs.meaning: Even if you haven't prepared enough food (e.g. guests arrive unexpectedly during a family meal), this expresses the idea of sharing with everyone regardless of the quantity.

observations: Hospitality is very much part of Malagasy culture, and often surpasses the expectation of foreigners.
Meal sharing goes even further: if the host has just finished their meal and visitors arrive unexpectedly, he/she will still cook a meal for them.
If the host is still eating and visitors arrive unexpectedly, he/she will share his/her meal with them.
If the visitors are just about to leave before the meal is ready, they are told to wait for the meal: 'Miandrasa sakafo' (off) or 'Mandesa hagniny' (tsm).
This practice is much more common in the villages.

In general the practice is very much in decline, particularly in the cities and among young people. However, it is still good to be aware of the strong emphasis on food and sharing in Malagasy culture.

lessons.title: Introducing yourself (Introduction-Lesson 3)
grammar_notes: To express the negative form of any sentence, add 'tsy' at the beginning (e.g. TSY MANAMBADY ZAHO = I am not married; not having children works the same way).
Beware: 'tsy' is not the same as 'tsisy'. 'Tsy' means not, whereas 'tsisy' means nothing.
'Mananjanaka zaho' = I have children (manan- + zanaka).
There are two words for children: 'zanaka' refers to children in relation to their parents; 'zaza' refers to children in the general sense.

In official Malagasy, saying 'my name is ...' and 'my job is ...' are inverted (the noun comes first, then 'no', then the possessive form). Tsimihety keeps possessive-first order: Anarako (name) (Tsm) vs (name) no anarako (Off); Asako (job) (Tsm) vs (job) no asako (Off).
APPENDIX - Basic grammar rules:
Rule 1: The subject of the sentence is at the END instead of the beginning (e.g. 'Avy any Angletera zaho' = I am from England, with zaho = I at the end).
Rule 2: 'to be' or 'to have' does not exist in the Malagasy language (e.g. 'I am from England' has no 'am').
Rule 3: Nouns do not have singular/plural forms (e.g. 'mananjanaka ray' = I have one child vs 'mananjanaka roa' = I have two children - only the number changes).
Rule 4: Similar to English, and unlike French, grammatical gender does not exist - no struggling with masculine and feminine forms.
Rule 5: Malagasy uses possessive suffixes. When connected to a noun or adjective, they give a sense of possession (see possessive tables).
Rule: Unlike French, there are no complex verb conjugations in Malagasy - no 'être' and 'avoir' conjugations.

Rule: Like English, there are verb tenses, but much simpler. Most verbs begin with the letter 'm'. For the past tense, 'm' is replaced with 'n'. For the future tense, 'm' is replaced with 'h' (e.g. miasa/niasa/hiasa zaho).

Rule: TSY means 'no/not' and TSISY means 'nothing', which can be quite confusing. To combine with another word, the rule is: Tsy + verb/adjective (e.g. Tsy miasa = not working); Tsisy + noun (e.g. Tsisy asa = no work).
cultural_notes: It is important to know how to introduce yourself when you arrive in Madagascar. One can talk about anything, but in practice some things are essential: saying your name, where you are from and what you do for a living.
After the obligatory introduction, you can talk about anything you like - for example your family, your spouse and children.
Malagasy society generally favours marriage and having children. If you are in neither of these categories, it might be difficult to avoid feeling a bit second-class.
So, if you don't know someone that well, it's probably not a good idea to ask if they are married or how many children they have!
In Malagasy, the word for boy, man and male are the same (lehilahy/lalahy); likewise for girl/woman/female (vehivavy/vaiavy).

lessons.title: Going to the market (Introduction-Lesson 4)
grammar_notes: 'Ve' is an interrogative particle which is very useful. You add it to a closed question to elicit a 'yes' or 'no' answer. Think of it as a word to replace a rising intonation when you ask a question. (Misy ... ve? = Is there ...?)
Rule 1 (numbers): Malagasy numbers are read from RIGHT to LEFT.
Rule 2 (numbers): The use of the connector 'and' is replaced with: AMBIN'NY for numbers between 11 and 19; AMBY for numbers between 21 and 199; SY for numbers beyond 200.
When counting quantities of items, the number follows the noun and unit (e.g. atody telo = 3 eggs; siramamy 3 kilao = 3 kilos of sugar).
Adjectives come after the noun (e.g. tongolo be = big onions, be = big) - relevant to the exercise 'How much are the big onions?'.
cultural_notes: Money: 1 Ar = 1 ariary. Ariary x 5 = Franc Malagasy.
When talking about money, 'ariary' is used with 10 Ar (ariary folo) and 100 Ar (ariary zato) only. For all other values the word is dropped, e.g. 200 Ar = roanjato.
In the market, prices generally start from about 100 Ar.
Malagasy Franc was replaced by Ariary in 2005 at a rate of 5 francs = 1 Ar. Hence, you will still find vendors quoting prices in Francs, especially to foreigners.
Always check if it's Francs or Ariary, and know your 5 times table well!
If the price is not displayed, do ask. The price is usually quoted in Ariary.
Even though there is no physical shop, 'mandroso' is used to invite the customer to approach and make their purchase.

lessons.title: Going to church (Introduction-Lesson 5)
grammar_notes: Reminder from Lesson 3: in Malagasy, most verbs begin with the letter 'm'. For the past tense, 'm' is replaced with 'n'. For the future tense, 'm' is replaced with 'h'. E.g. Mitsangana -> Hitsangana; Mihira -> Hihira.
You will hear the pronoun ANTSIKA (tsm) / ISIKA (off) (inclusive we) used a lot during the church service.

ORDINAL NUMBERS: We learnt cardinal numbers in lesson 4 (iray, roa, telo etc.). To refer to numbers that denote position or order, add the word 'FAHA' to the number, e.g. Faharoa (second), Fahatelo (third).
The exceptions are 'first' and 'last': we say VOALOHANY for 'first' and FARANY for 'last'. Faha-iray does not exist!

In Malagasy, ordinal numbering is used for Bible references and songs: where English says 'John chapter THREE verse SIXTEEN', Malagasy says it like 'John chapter THIRD verse SIXTEENTH' - JAONA TOKO FAHATELO ANDININY FAHA ENINA AMBIN'NY FOLO (John 3:16).
The same ordinal usage applies to verses in a song: ASAFA 34, 1st and 2nd verses = ASAFA FAHA EFATRA AMBY TELOPOLO ANDININY VOALOHANY SY FAHAROA.
In church, just pay attention to the word 'FAHA': it precedes every number you hear to convert it into an ordinal number.
Numbering systems in Malagasy can broadly be categorised into 4 groups: nominal, cardinal, frequency (number), and 'by (number)' (e.g. animals entering two by two into Noah's ark).

Frequency / 'by-number' questions and answers table: Question 'Firy?' -> Answer 'Roa' (two, cardinal); Question 'Fahafiry?' -> Answer 'Faharoa' (second, ordinal); Question 'Impiry?' -> Answer 'Indroa' (twice, frequency); Question 'Tsifirifiry' -> Answer 'Tsiroaroa' (two by two, by-number).
cultural_notes: Lesson 5 walks through a typical Baptist church service (Bako is a member of a Baptist church), so that you do not get lost on your first Sunday.

There are two main hymn books: FFPM (Fiombonan'ny Fiangonana Protestanta eto Madagasikara) - the official hymn book of Protestants throughout Madagascar; and ASAFA - the official hymn book of Baptist churches in Madagascar. There is also the Fihirana FANAMPINY, also referred to as the second volume of FFPM.
Church services (fanompoam-pivavahana) usually start at 9am.

Typical order of a Baptist service: 1. Fiderana (worship: sing, pray, read God's word, give a testimony), 2. Fanatitra (offering), 3. Anjara ho an'ny ankizy (children's lesson), 4. Vakiteny (Bible reading, usually the sermon passage), 5. Toriteny (sermon), 6. Filazana vaovao (announcements - includes welcoming first-time visitors, who usually stand up and give a short KABARY, see lesson 1a), 7. Tsodrano (benediction, usually a blessing from scripture), 8. Mifandray tanana (shaking hands with everyone) before parting.
Sunday school is usually at 8am before the service, and communion is after the service.
Being a Christian majority nation, it is quite easy to make a distinction in Madagascar between those who go to church (not necessarily Christians) and those who do not.
Malagasies believe in the existence of the greatest of gods, the Creator God (ZAGNAHARY / ANDRIAMANITRA), with different attributes such as God who blesses, protects, sees everything, etc.

In general, Malagasies believe that those who die 'are not dead' but are in a better place, somewhere between God and the living. Deceased people are said to be 'called by their fathers' or 'they have fallen asleep'.

You might remember the numbers by now, but hearing them reeled off quickly at church requires quite a bit more practice and time! Trying to figure out which song or passage is being referenced during the service is really a challenge, but don't lose heart, as you'll soon get used to it.

lessons.title: Visiting a village (Introduction-Lesson 6)
grammar_notes: ADJECTIVES: to construct a sentence with adjectives, the rule is the same as for verbs. There is no 'IS/ARE' in Malagasy sentences. The structure is: ADJECTIVE + NOUN/PRONOUN (e.g. MADIO ny rivotra = the air is clean; VAOVAO ny sakafo = the food is fresh; TSARA TAREHY ny kintana = the stars are beautiful).
To pose a question with an adjective, there are 3 ways. Example with 'the air is clean':
Way 1: MANAHOANA (off) / MANAKORY (tsm) + NOUN/PRONOUN? -> Answer: (ADJECTIVE). E.g. Manahoana/Manakory ny rivotra? Madio. (How is the air? Clean.)

Way 2: ADJECTIVE + VE + NOUN/PRONOUN? -> Answer: (YES/NO + ADJECTIVE). E.g. Madio ve ny rivotra? Eny (off)/Ia (tsm), madio - or - Tsia (off)/ehe (tsm), tsy madio. (Is the air clean? Yes, clean / No, not clean.)
Way 3: INONA NO (off) / INO (tsm) + ADJECTIVE? -> Answer: (NOUN/PRONOUN). E.g. Inona no/Ino madio? Ny rivotra. (What is clean? The air.)

Replacing the noun with a pronoun (example: TSARA TAREHY IZY = He/she is beautiful), the question structure is the same: IZA NO (off) / ZOVY (tsm) + ADJECTIVE? E.g. Iza no/Zovy tsara tarehy? Izy. (Who is beautiful? He/she is.)
REVISION OF RULE FOR TSY/TSISY (lesson 1 revision): 1. TSY + ADJECTIVE = e.g. Tsy betsaka (not many); 2. TSISY + NOUN = e.g. Tsisy tabataba (no noise).
Ve = interrogative particle for asking a question.
Fa maninona (off) / manino (tsm) = why (question words revision from lesson 1).
cultural_notes: During your time in Mandritsara, you might have the opportunity of visiting villages around the region - a day trip on foot/motorbike, or a few days with the community team by helicopter.
It is helpful to equip yourself with some basic vocabulary, including a few adjectives that might come in handy.
Village life observations from the text: few vehicles, clean air, spacious land, generally fresh food, little noise, beautiful sky and stars at night.

cultural_notes: Family size tends to be large in Madagascar. Relationships between family members are important in daily life, through good and bad times.
Starting a family is one of the main purposes of marriage - it is challenging being single or childless in the Malagasy culture.
Malagasies consider: uncles/aunties like parents; cousins like siblings; nephews/nieces like one's own children.
Marriage is a family affair, not just between the couple.
Specific terms for family members are very complicated in Malagasy, and Tsimihety is even more complicated than official Malagasy.

lessons.title: The House (Ny trano off / Ny tragno tsm)
cultural_notes: Traditional Malagasy houses are built with wood or raw earth. The roof is made of tafo bozaka (thatch) or tafo taila (off) / tafo tanimanga (tsm) - tile / terracotta.
Traditional houses typically consist of 1 or 2 rooms: one room with a kitchen corner, or 2 rooms, one of which is a lakozia (kitchen) and the other a tranobe (off) / tragnobe (tsm) - the large room.
All doors of traditional Malagasy houses should always face west so that the house can benefit from the sunlight until sunset.
Malagasy people often use the cardinal points North (avaratra), South (atsimo), West (andrefana), and East (atsinanana) for orientation.
In Malagasy, tanana or vohitra means town or village. The size of a town is defined by the number of roofs or kitchens.
Grammar rule from the lesson: 'Mi-' is used for intransitive verbs and 'Ma-' for transitive verbs in relation to houses or doors (e.g. mivoha = to be open vs mamoha = to open).

lessons.title: Weather & Climate (Ny andro sy ny toetr'andro)
cultural_notes: For Malagasy people in general, when listening to the weather forecast, 'good weather' means sunny and without rain. However, during the planting season, rain is needed, and farmers do not agree with the concept of 'bad weather' (with rain).
The word 'NY ANDRO' (which means day) is used to describe the weather or climate.

Madagascar is in the southern hemisphere, so the characteristics of the seasons are different from those in the northern hemisphere. The words for the four Malagasy seasons are: fahavaratra (off) / asaratra (tsm) = summer; fararana = autumn; ririnina (off) / maintany (tsm) = winter; lohataona = spring.
Madagascar has two main climates: MAFANA sy MANDO (hot and humid) from October to March, and MANINTSY sy MAINA (cool and dry) from April to September.

lessons.title: Jobs (Ny asa)
cultural_notes: Many job names in Malagasy are derived from verbs, generally by changing the initial letter M of the verb to Mp (with some exceptions), e.g. mianatra (to study) becomes mpianatra (student).
Possessive adjectives in Malagasy are added as suffixes to nouns, e.g. asako = my job, asanao = your job.

lessons.title: Clothing and Colours (Ny fitafiana sy ny loko)
cultural_notes: Clothing in Madagascar varies depending on the region of origin. Most people wear lamba (traditional cloth) by either mitafy (draping) or misikina (wrapping it around themselves).
There are clothes worn daily, some reserved for celebrations, and others for funerals or mourning. During mourning, people often wear dark or white clothing, with red being rarely used.
As Madagascar is a hot country, there aren't specific clothes for cold weather. Instead, people wear more layers to keep warm.
Women: generally have long hair, sometimes braided, and often wear dresses. In many regions, they also wear lambahoany (a type of traditional cloth).
Men: tend to wear hats more frequently than women.
In some regions, people remove their shoes before entering a house.
According to Malagasy culture, hats are removed when entering a house, singing the national anthem, or encountering a funeral procession.
Dark-coloured clothes are typically worn during mourning, while bright-coloured ones are worn for celebrations.

Grammar note: certain colour names can be duplicated to signify a more vivid or purer shade, e.g. fotsy = fotsifotsy, mena = menamena, mavo = mavomavo, mainty = maintimainty, maitso = maitsomaitso, manga = mangamanga.

lessons.title: Parts of the Body - Diseases (Ny aretina)
cultural_notes: Madagascar does not have enough medical infrastructure or doctors, especially in villages far from the cities. Many people do not have the budget for healthcare. Consequently people rely on traditional medicine (herbal teas, massages, etc.).

Madagascar has many medicinal plants, and their names and uses are passed down orally. Some remedies are effective, others are not, and some can even be toxic depending on preparation and dosage. Some pharmaceutical laboratories have begun to study and use these plants.
The word MARARY can mean: ny marary (noun) = the patient; ny marary (noun) = pain; marary (adjective) = painful.

There are three common ways to describe being sick in Malagasy: 1. Using 'voan'ny' (off) / 'azon'ny' (tsm) + disease name to say 'I have a ...'; 2. Using 'marary' + body part to say 'I have pain in ...'; 3. Using adjectives and verbs (e.g. mafana hoditra izy = he has a fever, lit. hot skin)

lessons.title: Fruits and Vegetables (Ny voankazo sy ny legioma)
cultural_notes: Madagascar is a large tropical island where more than 80% of Malagasy households work in agriculture. For some it's their main source of income; for others it's a secondary activity. The primary crop is rice.

Each region of Madagascar is known for specific crops, depending on its climate (hot, cold, humid, etc.) and soil type (volcanic, sandy, clay, etc.). Even in the southern regions, which face significant rainfall challenges, fruits and legumes (dry grain vegetables) are abundant.
The central, northern, and eastern regions are rich in fruits, while vegetables are plentiful in the highlands. Wild fruits are also part of the landscape.
Madagascar's lychee is well recognized in some European countries and neighbouring islands.
Fruits and vegetables are seasonal. The only fruit available year-round is bananas. Fresh grain legumes can be purchased during their season, while dried ones are available year-round.
The Malagasy consume fruits fresh and vegetables either raw or cooked, often served with rice.

cultural_notes: Most fresh vegetables are seasonal, but dried-grain vegetables can be found all year round. They are preserved by harvesting the grains when mature and drying them. They are typically eaten with rice.

lessons.title: Animals (Ny biby)
cultural_notes: The daily life of Malagasy people is closely linked with insects and animals, wild or domesticated. Farmers often engage in animal husbandry alongside crop farming. Since rice is the staple, without the zebu there would be no rice paddies except with a great deal of extra work.

Animals play many roles: companions like the cat and dog; protectors like the dog; sources of food (meat, eggs, honey, locusts, etc.); sources of fertiliser; work animals like the zebu; means of transport; sources of income for the family and the country's economy; indicators of time (the first crowing of the rooster is at 3 a.m.); some transmit diseases like mosquitoes, or are pests like locusts.
Malagasy people are superstitious: seeing certain birds like crows or owls has a particular meaning.

The zebu has important roles at all stages of life, from birth to funerals, even after death: they work the fields; are a source of meat, fertiliser, milk, horns, and skin for industry; are a symbol of wealth and success; are a form of savings (in difficult times such as illness, zebus are sold to obtain money); are a means of transport harnessed to carts, replacing cars in rural areas; and are used in culture (sports, sacrifices, wedding ceremonies, funerals, national holidays, New Year in certain regions).
In some ethnic groups, a boy only becomes a man after stealing his first zebu.

In certain ethnic groups in southern Madagascar, when a man from the Mahafaly ethnic group dies, his zebu herd is sacrificed before burying him, with the skulls and horns hanging on his tomb. The people of the village eat the sacrificed meat. In this case, there is no inheritance of the herd for the children; they must create their own herd.
In some regions, during the wake or wedding, one or more zebus are killed to feed the village, family, or guests.
Zebu sacrifice is also important in certain regions during the 'Famadihana' (turning of the dead) ceremony.
In certain regions, the man gives a zebu as a 'Moletry' dowry to the bride's family.
In Malagasy, for the names of most animals the word 'vavy' (female) is added for the female, 'lahy' (male) for the male, and 'kely' (small) or 'zanaka' (child) for the young, e.g. akoho (chicken).
Madagascar has endemic animals like lemurs, but there are no venomous animals.

lessons.title: Telling the Time (Ny ora sy ny fotoana)
cultural_notes: The concept of time or the hour is one of the causes of frustration or misunderstanding for foreigners who work with Malagasy people or live in Madagascar.

There is an expression: 'Fotoan-gasy' (Malagasy time), and 'Manao fotoan-gasy ny Malagasy' (Malagasy people are not on time). It's 50% true - 50% false, because the two groups think with two different systems: foreigners have the hour and use a watch, but Malagasy people have time and use other systems like shadows, life events, and animal calls. That doesn't mean Malagasy people don't use watches.

Examples of Malagasy time concepts: A doctor telling a patient to return at 2 p.m. finds it more effective to say 'Come back after lunch' - in that case the patient might arrive even earlier. Waiting is not a big issue for Malagasy people.
When a Malagasy person gives someone an appointment they say 'You can come after 4 because I won't be there before' - not a precise time like '4:30'.
'How long was your journey?' - 'We left when the first rooster crowed and arrived at lunchtime.' - no number shows the trip's length in that answer.
'How many days were you coughing?' - 'Since Tuesday last week.'

Time is deeply tied to the environment and daily life of Malagasy people (most of whom are farmers): they use ALOKA (off) / KANDINDAGNA (tsm) = shadow (shadow position helps determine whether it's nearly midday or already afternoon), MASOANDRO (off) / MASÔVA (tsm) = sun (position and movement), FEON-BIBY = animal sounds, and daily activities (e.g. pounding rice, cows leaving or returning).
FAMANTARANANDRO (official) means 'to know the day' and refers to a watch or clock. In Tsimihety, 'montre' (French loanword) is the only word used for watch/clock.
'Minitra' (minute) and 'segondra' (second) are only used when talking about durations, not for telling the time.
To express the time, Malagasy uses the numbers from 1 to 12, relying on context or adding a time-of-day word (maraina, atoandro, tolakandro, hariva, alina) to indicate morning, noon, evening, etc.

Traditional clock-time expressions tied to daily life: 00:00 misasakalina (midnight); 02:00 maneno sahona (frogs croaking); 03:00 maneno akoho tokana (rooster crows once); 04:00 magiran-dratsy / mazava ratsy (dawn); 05:00 mifoha olo-mazoto (hard-working people wake up); 06:00 vaky masoandro (sunrise); 08:00 mivoaka omby (zebus come out of the pen); 09:00 mivoaka omby tera-bao (cow with calf comes out); 12:00 mitataovovonana (the sun is at the roof's highest point = noon); 13:00 mihilana ny andro (the day starts to lean = afternoon); 15:00 anpitotoam-bary ny andro (time when women pound rice); 17:00 mody omby (zebus come home); 18:00 maty masoandro (the sun dies = sunset); 20:00 manokom-bary olona (people cook dinner); 21:00 homam-bary olona (dinnertime); 21:30 tapi-mandry olona (everyone sleeps); 22:00 mivoaka mpamosavy (witches come out).

lessons.title: Directions 1 - Asking for Directions (Manontany sy manoro làlana/na toerana)
cultural_notes: Distance is relative: what some people call 'far', others call 'close', depending on their habits of travel.

In rural areas, kilometres are not commonly used to describe distance. Instead, people speak in terms of time using the word ADINY (off) / LERA (tsm) = hour. Example: 'làlana adiny 3' (off) = 'làlagna 3 lera' (tsm) - a 3-hour journey (by foot or vehicle).
To indicate a location, a place, or a region, Malagasy people often use the cardinal points (avaratra = North, atsimo = South, andrefana = West, atsinanana = East).
Both 'mpivarotra' and 'fivarotana' are used for shops/sellers.

lessons.title: Directions 2 - Asking for and Giving Directions (continued)
cultural_notes: In Madagascar, only in large towns do streets usually have names or numbers. In most places, people use landmarks instead.
When asking, Malagasy speakers always use azafady (please) first, then either ask the question directly or begin with an introductory phrase like 'Could you show/tell me ...'.

lessons.title: At School (Any an-tsekoly)
cultural_notes: Under the reign of King Radama I (1810-1828), the French Robin and Rev. Jones of the London Missionary Society (LMS) founded the first schools in Madagascar in 1820, at the initiative of a king who wanted closer ties with Europe through religious missionaries.

Although every person has the right to education, teaching, and training, access to education remains a challenge for different reasons: parental poverty, a bad harvest, early marriage, lack of nearby infrastructure, or competing priorities. There are still those who are illiterate or leave school early, and the level of schooling remains unequal across the country.
State school starts at age 6, private school at age 3. University begins at around age 18. There are three official exams: at age 10, 14, and 18.

lessons.title: Chores (Ny raharaha ao an-trano)
cultural_notes: Many Malagasy families still live from farming, livestock, fishing, and crafts. The tasks of each family member vary according to geographical, economic, social, and family circumstances.

Women more often stay at home, looking after the household and children, at least when the children are young, or they work from home to earn money. Traditionally, Malagasy women are responsible for managing the home and finances, the family's wellbeing, organising daily life, and the care and education of the children. Some also do gardening, sewing, or weaving. Men (the head of the family) are responsible for providing for and protecting the family, and making important decisions, though men can help and participate in household tasks.
More typically feminine tasks: preparing meals, cleaning the house, doing the laundry, fetching water, looking after young children, and tending the farmyard animals.
More typically masculine tasks: building and repairing the house, looking after the zebus, collecting firewood, and working in the fields.

When children are young they are taught traditional values, social rules, and the skills needed to succeed in life - they are already being prepared for their future roles. This is visible in play: boys make omby tanimanga (zebus made of clay); girls play tsikonona (cooking, but in small quantities).
Children participate in household chores according to their age, and sometimes, unfortunately, children have to help their parents by working.

lessons.title: The Daily Routine (Ny andavanandro)
cultural_notes: Every day we do almost the same things: get up, get ready, eat, go to work or school. But not everyone has the same daily routine - it depends on a person's activity and where they live.

Many Malagasy people are farmers: they get up before sunrise and start work while it is still cool, and they go to bed early. Their routine is more physical and seasonal, depending on the climate, and farmers do not do just one job - they look after animals, work in the fields, repair tools, sell produce, and listen to the radio for the news and serials with the family.
Language structure notes: MANDEHA + verb = 'go + verb' (e.g. mandeha miasa = go to work); you can join routine sentences with the conjunctions 'SY' = and and 'AVY EO' = then.

cultural_notes: NB from the lesson: In Malagasy, times are expressed from 1 to 12. To tell them apart, the part of the day is added after the number, such as maraina (morning) or hariva (afternoon/even). Adding the word 'ora' (hour) after the number is optional and does not change how the time is understood.

lessons.title: Transport (Ny fitaterana)
cultural_notes: In the past in Madagascar, people travelled mostly on foot. Kings and nobles used the 'filanjana', a chair carried by men. Goods were carried by porters, or in carts pulled by zebu. Later the choices became wide: rail, road, sea and river, and air. Sometimes the fare is fixed, sometimes negotiable.

The taxi-brousse is very typical for linking the different towns and villages of the big island. It is inexpensive, can carry many passengers and their luggage, and can cover long distances even on difficult roads.
Some means of transport, such as the motorbike or the cart, can provide transport in remote areas that are hard to reach. Pirogues and boats are used in places beside rivers and the sea.

Some names of means of transport are foreign words or Malagasy-ised words, such as 'taxi' and 'kamiao'. Others describe what the thing is, e.g. fiarandalamby (fiara + làlana + vy): a vehicle (fiara) whose road (làlana) is made of iron (vy); fiaramanidina (fiara + manidina): a vehicle (fiara) that flies (manidina).
Grammar: the verb MANDEHA (to go / to take) is used before the means of transport or travel, e.g. 'mandeha lakana' = to go by pirogue.

lessons.title: Transport - Dialogues (Fifampiresahana sy voambolana)
cultural_notes: Fare-setting culture from the taxi dialogue: after agreeing on the price (here 10,000 Ar / 20,000 Ar per person), payment is settled directly with cash ('Ity ny volanao / Ity ny vola' = here is the money).
Politeness formulas used throughout: azafady (please/excuse me), tompoko (sir/madam), misaotra (betsaka) (thank you very much), tsisy fisaorana (you're welcome), and soava dia (have a good journey).
Note from the lesson: to understand the dialogues, listen to them and then repeat them; you can take useful expressions from them.

culture.note: Greeting in Toamasina (east coast port city): "Manakory e! Akory lahaly?!" — Hello! How are you?!
Greeting in Northern region (incl. the practice place area north): "Mbola tsara!" — Still well! (common northern greeting)
Greeting in Southern region: "Akory koahy! Finaritra!" — Hello there! Pleasure!
Greeting in Everywhere (pan-regional): "Salama" — Hello — understood everywhere
Use tompoko ('TOOM-pook', unisex: sir/madam) after a sentence when speaking to an elder or authority figure.
In Madagascar each region has its own greeting — learning the local one earns warm smiles.
Antananarivo means 'City of the Thousand' (arivo = thousand).
'Tsy misy' (there is nothing) is a polite reply to beggars.
Bargaining at markets: sellers expect it; start lower and increase in small amounts.
The traveler's tree (ravinala) holds drinkable water in its trunk — a living symbol of Malagasy hospitality.
the tutor, has been a language tutor in the region since 2008, teaching missionaries and visitors to the Hopitaly Vaovao Mahafaly project.
The dialect spoken in the region is called Tsimihety, but official Malagasy is widely spoken there as well.
in the region the most common way of greeting each other is by saying 'Salama Tompoko', literally 'hello, sir'.
When one arrives at a friend's house, the guest initiates the greeting at the door by saying out loud 'Haody!', much like a knock on the door.
A 'Kabary' is where both the guest and host take turns to give a short speech.

Malagasy Kabary originated as a highly poeticised speech performed in front of an audience. Today it is an integral part of social life, used in social events like festivities, ceremonies and funerals. Informally, people use it to convey thanks or welcome at dinner parties or gatherings.
If a guest is invited to a meal, the host never asks 'in vaovao' (what's new), as the intention for the visit is obvious.
There are 18 tribes spread across 22 regions in Madagascar.
Other ways of saying hello in Madagascar vary by region: 'Manao ahoana' (Central, e.g. Tana), 'Salama' (North/Central), 'Akory' (East/South), 'Miarahaba' (Central).
There are a number of ways to say goodbye in Malagasy; the most common are 'Veloma tompoko', 'Veloma e', 'Mazotoa', and 'Amin'ny manaraka indray'.
In Tsimihety, sometimes the 'n' consonant has a nasal sound which can be written as n̈ or ñ. In these lesson notes it is spelled 'gn' for convenience (e.g. volagna, taogno, amaraigny).
Although 'misaotra' is sufficient, saying 'MISAOTRA BETSAKA' is more polite.
You will invariably hear the word 'azafady' used a lot; it is an extremely useful word.

Body language (giving/receiving a gift): one usually stretches out both hands to express politeness. in the region, when one gives something or says 'misaotra', one usually bends the knee slightly as a sign of reverence.
Body language (walking past people): slightly bow your body and stretch your right hand out.
'MIALA TSINY' is another way of apologising over something trivial. For a serious offence you would literally be asking for forgiveness: 'MIFONA'. This is the term used in the Bible.
When invited with 'mandroso' to join a meal, the person is definitely not obliged to sit down and eat; they can simply respond 'Misaotra, mazotoa'.

It is important to know how to introduce yourself when you arrive in Madagascar. One can talk about anything, but in practice some things are essential: saying your name, where you are from and what you do for a living.
After the obligatory introduction, you can talk about anything you like - for example your family, your spouse and children.
Malagasy society generally favours marriage and having children. If you are in neither of these categories, it might be difficult to avoid feeling a bit second-class.
So, if you don't know someone that well, it's probably not a good idea to ask if they are married or how many children they have!
In Malagasy, the word for boy, man and male are the same (lehilahy/lalahy); likewise for girl/woman/female (vehivavy/vaiavy).
Money: 1 Ar = 1 ariary. Ariary x 5 = Franc Malagasy.
When talking about money, 'ariary' is used with 10 Ar (ariary folo) and 100 Ar (ariary zato) only. For all other values the word is dropped, e.g. 200 Ar = roanjato.
In the market, prices generally start from about 100 Ar.
Malagasy Franc was replaced by Ariary in 2005 at a rate of 5 francs = 1 Ar. Hence, you will still find vendors quoting prices in Francs, especially to foreigners.
Always check if it's Francs or Ariary, and know your 5 times table well!
If the price is not displayed, do ask. The price is usually quoted in Ariary.
Even though there is no physical shop, 'mandroso' is used to invite the customer to approach and make their purchase.

Lesson 5 walks through a typical Baptist church service ( is a member of a Baptist church), so that you do not get lost on your first Sunday.

There are two main hymn books: FFPM (Fiombonan'ny Fiangonana Protestanta eto Madagasikara) - the official hymn book of Protestants throughout Madagascar; and ASAFA - the official hymn book of Baptist churches in Madagascar. There is also the Fihirana FANAMPINY, also referred to as the second volume of FFPM.
Church services (fanompoam-pivavahana) usually start at 9am.

Typical order of a Baptist service: 1. Fiderana (worship: sing, pray, read God's word, give a testimony), 2. Fanatitra (offering), 3. Anjara ho an'ny ankizy (children's lesson), 4. Vakiteny (Bible reading, usually the sermon passage), 5. Toriteny (sermon), 6. Filazana vaovao (announcements - includes welcoming first-time visitors, who usually stand up and give a short KABARY, see lesson 1a), 7. Tsodrano (benediction, usually a blessing from scripture), 8. Mifandray tanana (shaking hands with everyone) before parting.
Sunday school is usually at 8am before the service, and communion is after the service.
Being a Christian majority nation, it is quite easy to make a distinction in Madagascar between those who go to church (not necessarily Christians) and those who do not.
Malagasies believe in the existence of the greatest of gods, the Creator God (ZAGNAHARY / ANDRIAMANITRA), with different attributes such as God who blesses, protects, sees everything, etc.

In general, Malagasies believe that those who die 'are not dead' but are in a better place, somewhere between God and the living. Deceased people are said to be 'called by their fathers' or 'they have fallen asleep'.

You might remember the numbers by now, but hearing them reeled off quickly at church requires quite a bit more practice and time! Trying to figure out which song or passage is being referenced during the service is really a challenge, but don't lose heart, as you'll soon get used to it.
During your time in the region, you might have the opportunity of visiting villages around the region - a day trip on foot/motorbike, or a few days with the community team by helicopter.
It is helpful to equip yourself with some basic vocabulary, including a few adjectives that might come in handy.
Village life observations from the text: few vehicles, clean air, spacious land, generally fresh food, little noise, beautiful sky and stars at night.
Family size tends to be large in Madagascar. Relationships between family members are important in daily life, through good and bad times.
Starting a family is one of the main purposes of marriage - it is challenging being single or childless in the Malagasy culture.
Malagasies consider: uncles/aunties like parents; cousins like siblings; nephews/nieces like one's own children.
Marriage is a family affair, not just between the couple.
Specific terms for family members are very complicated in Malagasy, and Tsimihety is even more complicated than official Malagasy.
Naming conventions of relationships between family members are illustrated with family tree diagrams covering three generations and siblings.

Traditional Malagasy houses are built with wood or raw earth. The roof is made of tafo bozaka (thatch) or tafo taila (off) / tafo tanimanga (tsm) - tile / terracotta.
Traditional houses typically consist of 1 or 2 rooms: one room with a kitchen corner, or 2 rooms, one of which is a lakozia (kitchen) and the other a tranobe (off) / tragnobe (tsm) - the large room.
All doors of traditional Malagasy houses should always face west so that the house can benefit from the sunlight until sunset.
Malagasy people often use the cardinal points North (avaratra), South (atsimo), West (andrefana), and East (atsinanana) for orientation.
In Malagasy, tanana or vohitra means town or village. The size of a town is defined by the number of roofs or kitchens.
Grammar rule from the lesson: 'Mi-' is used for intransitive verbs and 'Ma-' for transitive verbs in relation to houses or doors (e.g. mivoha = to be open vs mamoha = to open).

For Malagasy people in general, when listening to the weather forecast, 'good weather' means sunny and without rain. However, during the planting season, rain is needed, and farmers do not agree with the concept of 'bad weather' (with rain).
The word 'NY ANDRO' (which means day) is used to describe the weather or climate.

Madagascar is in the southern hemisphere, so the characteristics of the seasons are different from those in the northern hemisphere. The words for the four Malagasy seasons are: fahavaratra (off) / asaratra (tsm) = summer; fararana = autumn; ririnina (off) / maintany (tsm) = winter; lohataona = spring.
Madagascar has two main climates: MAFANA sy MANDO (hot and humid) from October to March, and MANINTSY sy MAINA (cool and dry) from April to September.
Sentence-building tip from the lesson: to set the kitchen verbs into sentences, start by asking 'Maninona izy?' (off) / 'Manino izy?' (tsm) - What is he/she doing?
Many job names in Malagasy are derived from verbs, generally by changing the initial letter M of the verb to Mp (with some exceptions), e.g. mianatra (to study) becomes mpianatra (student).
Possessive adjectives in Malagasy are added as suffixes to nouns, e.g. asako = my job, asanao = your job.
Possessive suffix table from the lesson: aho/zaho + -ko (asako); ianao + -nao (asanao); izy + -ny (asany); izahay + -nay; isika + -ntsika; ianareo + -reo; izy ireo + -ny.
Clothing in Madagascar varies depending on the region of origin. Most people wear lamba (traditional cloth) by either mitafy (draping) or misikina (wrapping it around themselves).
There are clothes worn daily, some reserved for celebrations, and others for funerals or mourning. During mourning, people often wear dark or white clothing, with red being rarely used.
As Madagascar is a hot country, there aren't specific clothes for cold weather. Instead, people wear more layers to keep warm.
Women: generally have long hair, sometimes braided, and often wear dresses. In many regions, they also wear lambahoany (a type of traditional cloth).
Men: tend to wear hats more frequently than women.
In some regions, people remove their shoes before entering a house.
According to Malagasy culture, hats are removed when entering a house, singing the national anthem, or encountering a funeral procession.
Dark-coloured clothes are typically worn during mourning, while bright-coloured ones are worn for celebrations.

Grammar note: certain colour names can be duplicated to signify a more vivid or purer shade, e.g. fotsy = fotsifotsy, mena = menamena, mavo = mavomavo, mainty = maintimainty, maitso = maitsomaitso, manga = mangamanga.

Learning technique from the lesson for body parts vocabulary: 1. listen repeatedly (e.g. maso = eye); 2. listen and point to the part on your body; 3. point and say ITY (this) or IRETO (these) in response to 'AIZA ny ...?' (Where is the ...?); 4. listen and repeat twice (maso >> maso, maso); 5. answer 'INONA ity / ireto?' (What is this / what are these?) with the body part name.

Madagascar does not have enough medical infrastructure or doctors, especially in villages far from the cities. Many people do not have the budget for healthcare. Consequently people rely on traditional medicine (herbal teas, massages, etc.).

Madagascar has many medicinal plants, and their names and uses are passed down orally. Some remedies are effective, others are not, and some can even be toxic depending on preparation and dosage. Some pharmaceutical laboratories have begun to study and use these plants.
The word MARARY can mean: ny marary (noun) = the patient; ny marary (noun) = pain; marary (adjective) = painful.

There are three common ways to describe being sick in Malagasy: 1. Using 'voan'ny' (off) / 'azon'ny' (tsm) + disease name to say 'I have a ...'; 2. Using 'marary' + body part to say 'I have pain in ...'; 3. Using adjectives and verbs (e.g. mafana hoditra izy = he has a fever, lit. hot skin)

Madagascar is a large tropical island where more than 80% of Malagasy households work in agriculture. For some it's their main source of income; for others it's a secondary activity. The primary crop is rice.

Each region of Madagascar is known for specific crops, depending on its climate (hot, cold, humid, etc.) and soil type (volcanic, sandy, clay, etc.). Even in the southern regions, which face significant rainfall challenges, fruits and legumes (dry grain vegetables) are abundant.
The central, northern, and eastern regions are rich in fruits, while vegetables are plentiful in the highlands. Wild fruits are also part of the landscape.
Madagascar's lychee is well recognized in some European countries and neighbouring islands.
Fruits and vegetables are seasonal. The only fruit available year-round is bananas. Fresh grain legumes can be purchased during their season, while dried ones are available year-round.
The Malagasy consume fruits fresh and vegetables either raw or cooked, often served with rice.

Most fresh vegetables are seasonal, but dried-grain vegetables can be found all year round. They are preserved by harvesting the grains when mature and drying them. They are typically eaten with rice.

The daily life of Malagasy people is closely linked with insects and animals, wild or domesticated. Farmers often engage in animal husbandry alongside crop farming. Since rice is the staple, without the zebu there would be no rice paddies except with a great deal of extra work.

Animals play many roles: companions like the cat and dog; protectors like the dog; sources of food (meat, eggs, honey, locusts, etc.); sources of fertiliser; work animals like the zebu; means of transport; sources of income for the family and the country's economy; indicators of time (the first crowing of the rooster is at 3 a.m.); some transmit diseases like mosquitoes, or are pests like locusts.
Malagasy people are superstitious: seeing certain birds like crows or owls has a particular meaning.

The zebu has important roles at all stages of life, from birth to funerals, even after death: they work the fields; are a source of meat, fertiliser, milk, horns, and skin for industry; are a symbol of wealth and success; are a form of savings (in difficult times such as illness, zebus are sold to obtain money); are a means of transport harnessed to carts, replacing cars in rural areas; and are used in culture (sports, sacrifices, wedding ceremonies, funerals, national holidays, New Year in certain regions).
In some ethnic groups, a boy only becomes a man after stealing his first zebu.

In certain ethnic groups in southern Madagascar, when a man from the Mahafaly ethnic group dies, his zebu herd is sacrificed before burying him, with the skulls and horns hanging on his tomb. The people of the village eat the sacrificed meat. In this case, there is no inheritance of the herd for the children; they must create their own herd.
In some regions, during the wake or wedding, one or more zebus are killed to feed the village, family, or guests.
Zebu sacrifice is also important in certain regions during the 'Famadihana' (turning of the dead) ceremony.
In certain regions, the man gives a zebu as a 'Moletry' dowry to the bride's family.
In Malagasy, for the names of most animals the word 'vavy' (female) is added for the female, 'lahy' (male) for the male, and 'kely' (small) or 'zanaka' (child) for the young, e.g. akoho (chicken).
Madagascar has endemic animals like lemurs, but there are no venomous animals.

The concept of time or the hour is one of the causes of frustration or misunderstanding for foreigners who work with Malagasy people or live in Madagascar.

There is an expression: 'Fotoan-gasy' (Malagasy time), and 'Manao fotoan-gasy ny Malagasy' (Malagasy people are not on time). It's 50% true - 50% false, because the two groups think with two different systems: foreigners have the hour and use a watch, but Malagasy people have time and use other systems like shadows, life events, and animal calls. That doesn't mean Malagasy people don't use watches.

Examples of Malagasy time concepts: A doctor telling a patient to return at 2 p.m. finds it more effective to say 'Come back after lunch' - in that case the patient might arrive even earlier. Waiting is not a big issue for Malagasy people.
When a Malagasy person gives someone an appointment they say 'You can come after 4 because I won't be there before' - not a precise time like '4:30'.
'How long was your journey?' - 'We left when the first rooster crowed and arrived at lunchtime.' - no number shows the trip's length in that answer.
'How many days were you coughing?' - 'Since Tuesday last week.'

Time is deeply tied to the environment and daily life of Malagasy people (most of whom are farmers): they use ALOKA (off) / KANDINDAGNA (tsm) = shadow (shadow position helps determine whether it's nearly midday or already afternoon), MASOANDRO (off) / MASÔVA (tsm) = sun (position and movement), FEON-BIBY = animal sounds, and daily activities (e.g. pounding rice, cows leaving or returning).
FAMANTARANANDRO (official) means 'to know the day' and refers to a watch or clock. In Tsimihety, 'montre' (French loanword) is the only word used for watch/clock.
'Minitra' (minute) and 'segondra' (second) are only used when talking about durations, not for telling the time.
To express the time, Malagasy uses the numbers from 1 to 12, relying on context or adding a time-of-day word (maraina, atoandro, tolakandro, hariva, alina) to indicate morning, noon, evening, etc.

Traditional clock-time expressions tied to daily life: 00:00 misasakalina (midnight); 02:00 maneno sahona (frogs croaking); 03:00 maneno akoho tokana (rooster crows once); 04:00 magiran-dratsy / mazava ratsy (dawn); 05:00 mifoha olo-mazoto (hard-working people wake up); 06:00 vaky masoandro (sunrise); 08:00 mivoaka omby (zebus come out of the pen); 09:00 mivoaka omby tera-bao (cow with calf comes out); 12:00 mitataovovonana (the sun is at the roof's highest point = noon); 13:00 mihilana ny andro (the day starts to lean = afternoon); 15:00 anpitotoam-bary ny andro (time when women pound rice); 17:00 mody omby (zebus come home); 18:00 maty masoandro (the sun dies = sunset); 20:00 manokom-bary olona (people cook dinner); 21:00 homam-bary olona (dinnertime); 21:30 tapi-mandry olona (everyone sleeps); 22:00 mivoaka mpamosavy (witches come out).
Distance is relative: what some people call 'far', others call 'close', depending on their habits of travel.

In rural areas, kilometres are not commonly used to describe distance. Instead, people speak in terms of time using the word ADINY (off) / LERA (tsm) = hour. Example: 'làlana adiny 3' (off) = 'làlagna 3 lera' (tsm) - a 3-hour journey (by foot or vehicle).
To indicate a location, a place, or a region, Malagasy people often use the cardinal points (avaratra = North, atsimo = South, andrefana = West, atsinanana = East).
Both 'mpivarotra' and 'fivarotana' are used for shops/sellers.
In Madagascar, only in large towns do streets usually have names or numbers. In most places, people use landmarks instead.
When asking, Malagasy speakers always use azafady (please) first, then either ask the question directly or begin with an introductory phrase like 'Could you show/tell me ...'.

Under the reign of King Radama I (1810-1828), the French Robin and Rev. Jones of the London Missionary Society (LMS) founded the first schools in Madagascar in 1820, at the initiative of a king who wanted closer ties with Europe through religious missionaries.

Although every person has the right to education, teaching, and training, access to education remains a challenge for different reasons: parental poverty, a bad harvest, early marriage, lack of nearby infrastructure, or competing priorities. There are still those who are illiterate or leave school early, and the level of schooling remains unequal across the country.
State school starts at age 6, private school at age 3. University begins at around age 18. There are three official exams: at age 10, 14, and 18.
Many Malagasy families still live from farming, livestock, fishing, and crafts. The tasks of each family member vary according to geographical, economic, social, and family circumstances.

Women more often stay at home, looking after the household and children, at least when the children are young, or they work from home to earn money. Traditionally, Malagasy women are responsible for managing the home and finances, the family's wellbeing, organising daily life, and the care and education of the children. Some also do gardening, sewing, or weaving. Men (the head of the family) are responsible for providing for and protecting the family, and making important decisions, though men can help and participate in household tasks.
More typically feminine tasks: preparing meals, cleaning the house, doing the laundry, fetching water, looking after young children, and tending the farmyard animals.
More typically masculine tasks: building and repairing the house, looking after the zebus, collecting firewood, and working in the fields.

When children are young they are taught traditional values, social rules, and the skills needed to succeed in life - they are already being prepared for their future roles. This is visible in play: boys make omby tanimanga (zebus made of clay); girls play tsikonona (cooking, but in small quantities).
Children participate in household chores according to their age, and sometimes, unfortunately, children have to help their parents by working.
Every day we do almost the same things: get up, get ready, eat, go to work or school. But not everyone has the same daily routine - it depends on a person's activity and where they live.

Many Malagasy people are farmers: they get up before sunrise and start work while it is still cool, and they go to bed early. Their routine is more physical and seasonal, depending on the climate, and farmers do not do just one job - they look after animals, work in the fields, repair tools, sell produce, and listen to the radio for the news and serials with the family.
Language structure notes: MANDEHA + verb = 'go + verb' (e.g. mandeha miasa = go to work); you can join routine sentences with the conjunctions 'SY' = and and 'AVY EO' = then.

NB from the lesson: In Malagasy, times are expressed from 1 to 12. To tell them apart, the part of the day is added after the number, such as maraina (morning) or hariva (afternoon/even). Adding the word 'ora' (hour) after the number is optional and does not change how the time is understood.

In the past in Madagascar, people travelled mostly on foot. Kings and nobles used the 'filanjana', a chair carried by men. Goods were carried by porters, or in carts pulled by zebu. Later the choices became wide: rail, road, sea and river, and air. Sometimes the fare is fixed, sometimes negotiable.

The taxi-brousse is very typical for linking the different towns and villages of the big island. It is inexpensive, can carry many passengers and their luggage, and can cover long distances even on difficult roads.
Some means of transport, such as the motorbike or the cart, can provide transport in remote areas that are hard to reach. Pirogues and boats are used in places beside rivers and the sea.

Some names of means of transport are foreign words or Malagasy-ised words, such as 'taxi' and 'kamiao'. Others describe what the thing is, e.g. fiarandalamby (fiara + làlana + vy): a vehicle (fiara) whose road (làlana) is made of iron (vy); fiaramanidina (fiara + manidina): a vehicle (fiara) that flies (manidina).
Grammar: the verb MANDEHA (to go / to take) is used before the means of transport or travel, e.g. 'mandeha lakana' = to go by pirogue.
NB: 'mandroso sy miverina' is a set expression for a return (round-trip) ticket, lit. 'going and returning'.

Fare-setting culture from the taxi dialogue: after agreeing on the price (here 10,000 Ar / 20,000 Ar per person), payment is settled directly with cash ('Ity ny volanao / Ity ny vola' = here is the money).
Politeness formulas used throughout: azafady (please/excuse me), tompoko (sir/madam), misaotra (betsaka) (thank you very much), tsisy fisaorana (you're welcome), and soava dia (have a good journey).
Note from the lesson: to understand the dialogues, listen to them and then repeat them; you can take useful expressions from them.
